# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

The **Living Studio desktop app** is the GUI product, but it ships as separate manual Tauri downloads and presently requires a Python/uv development environment, so it is not yet a turnkey end-user install. #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Default install locations (user-local)
INSTALL_ROOT="${AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR:-${XDG_DATA_HOME:-${HOME}/.local/share}/agentic-odi}"
BIN_DIR="${AGENTIC_ODI_BIN_DIR:-${XDG_BIN_HOME:-${HOME}/.local/bin}}"

BASE_URL_DEFAULT="https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases"
API_BASE_DEFAULT="https://api.github.com/repos/alehar9320/agentic-odi"

# The download directory must outlive main() so the EXIT trap can clean it up
# (`set -u` makes a function-local reference in a trap fatal).
TMPDIR_INSTALL=""
cleanup() { [[ -n "$TMPDIR_INSTALL" ]] && rm -rf "$TMPDIR_INSTALL"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

detect_os() {
  case "$(uname -s)" in
    Linux*)  echo "linux" ;;
    Darwin*) echo "macos" ;;
    *)       echo "linux" ;;
  esac
}

detect_arch() {
  local m
  m="$(uname -m)"
  case "$m" in
    x86_64|amd64|AMD64) echo "x86_64" ;;
    aarch64|arm64)      echo "arm64" ;;
    *)                  echo "$m" ;;
  esac
}

resolve_version() {
  if [[ -n "${AGENTIC_ODI_VERSION:-}" ]]; then
    echo "${AGENTIC_ODI_VERSION}"
    return
  fi
  local api_base
  api_base="${AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL:-${API_BASE_DEFAULT}}"
  if [[ "${api_base}" == http*://* ]] && [[ "${api_base}" != *api.github.com* ]]; then
    # Local test base; try to read version from a file if present? fallback to 0.1.0
    echo "0.1.0"
    return
  fi
  curl -fsSL "${API_BASE_DEFAULT}/releases/latest" | grep -o '"tag_name"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"[^"]*"' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)"/\1/' | sed 's/^v//'
}

# checksums.txt lists every platform's archive, but only this platform's archive
# is downloaded here, so verify that single entry instead of the whole file.
sha256_verify() {
  local file="$1"
  local checksums="$2"
  local name entry
  name="$(basename "$file")"
  if ! entry="$(awk -v name="$name" '$2 == name || $2 == "*" name { print; found = 1 } END { if (!found) exit 1 }' "$checksums")"; then
    echo "No checksum entry for $name in $(basename "$checksums")" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    if ! (cd "$(dirname "$file")" && printf '%s\n' "$entry" | sha256sum -c --quiet -); then
      echo "Checksum verification failed for $name" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    return
  fi
  if command -v shasum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    if ! (cd "$(dirname "$file")" && printf '%s\n' "$entry" | shasum -a 256 -c - >/dev/null 2>&1); then
      echo "Checksum verification failed for $name" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    return
  fi
  echo "Warning: no sha256 tool found; skipping verification" >&2
}

  os="$(detect_os)"
  arch="$(detect_arch)"
  version="$(resolve_version)"
  target="${os}_${arch}"

  archive_name="odi_${version}_${target}.tar.gz"
  checksums_name="checksums.txt"

  base="${AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL:-${BASE_URL_DEFAULT}}"
  if [[ "${base}" == *api.github.com* ]]; then
    base="${BASE_URL_DEFAULT}"
  fi
  local dl_base
  dl_base="${base}/download/v${version}"

  mkdir -p "$INSTALL_ROOT/versions" "$BIN_DIR"

  local tmpdir="$TMPDIR_INSTALL"

  curl -fsSL "${dl_base}/${archive_name}" -o "${tmpdir}/${archive_name}"
  curl -fsSL "${dl_base}/${checksums_name}" -o "${tmpdir}/${checksums_name}"

  sha256_verify "${tmpdir}/${archive_name}" "${tmpdir}/${checksums_name}"

  local ver_dir tmp_ver
  ver_dir="${INSTALL_ROOT}/versions/${version}"
  tmp_ver="${INSTALL_ROOT}/versions/.${version}.tmp.$$"
  rm -rf "$tmp_ver"
  mkdir -p "$tmp_ver"

  tar -xzf "${tmpdir}/${archive_name}" -C "$tmp_ver"
  rm -rf "$ver_dir"
  mv "$tmp_ver" "$ver_dir"

  local current_tmp
  current_tmp="${INSTALL_ROOT}/current.tmp.$$"
  ln -sfn "$ver_dir" "$current_tmp"
  mv -T "$current_tmp" "${INSTALL_ROOT}/current"

    ln -sfn "${INSTALL_ROOT}/current/odi" "${BIN_DIR}/${cmd}"
  done

  if [[ ! ":$PATH:" == *":${BIN_DIR}:"* ]]; then
    echo "Add ${BIN_DIR} to your PATH (export PATH=\"${BIN_DIR}:\$PATH\")"
  fi

  echo "Installed odi ${version} to ${ver_dir}"

)

EMOJI = re.compile("[\u2600-\u27bf\U0001f300-\U0001faff]")


class Doc(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.lang = None
        self.charset = False
        self.viewport = False
        self.title = ""
        self.ids: set[str] = set()
        self.hrefs: list[str] = []
        self.refs: list[str] = []
        self.headings: list[tuple[int, str]] = []
        self.tags: list[str] = []
        self.metas: dict[str, str] = {}
        self.theme_colors: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
        self.text: list[str] = []
        self._in_title = False
        self._heading: tuple[int, list[str]] | None = None

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        a = dict(attrs)
        self.tags.append(tag)
        if tag == "html":
            self.lang = a.get("lang")
        elif tag == "title":
            self._in_title = True
        elif tag == "meta":
            if a.get("charset"):
                self.charset = True
            if a.get("name") == "viewport":
                self.viewport = True
            if a.get("name") == "theme-color":
                self.theme_colors.append((a.get("content", ""), a.get("media", "")))
            key = a.get("property") or a.get("name")
            if key:
                self.metas[key] = a.get("content", "")
        elif tag == "a" and a.get("href"):
            self.hrefs.append(a["href"])
        elif tag in ("link", "script", "img"):
            ref = a.get("href") or a.get("src")
            if ref:
                self.refs.append(ref)
        if a.get("id"):
            self.ids.add(a["id"])
        if re.fullmatch(r"h[1-6]", tag):
            self._heading = (int(tag[1]), [])

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag == "title":
            self._in_title = False
        elif self._heading and tag == f"h{self._heading[0]}":
            level, parts = self._heading
            self.headings.append((level, " ".join("".join(parts).split())))
            self._heading = None

    def handle_data(self, data):
        self.text.append(data)
        if self._in_title:
            self.title += data
        if self._heading:
            self._heading[1].append(data)


def parse(name: str) -> Doc:
    doc = Doc()
    doc.feed((SITE / name).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return doc

# Installation

Prebuilt binaries are available for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Install the latest
release with one command:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

The installer places the binary under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/versions/<version>/`,
creates a `current` symlink, and symlinks `odi`, `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and
`agentic-odi` into `~/.local/bin/`.

If `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH, add it (e.g.,
`export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`). On Windows, the PowerShell installer
uses `~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\` and copies `.exe` files to
`~\AppData\Local\agentic-odi\bin\`.

## Update

By default, `odi` auto-checks for updates once every 24 hours and applies the
update on the next run (auto-update is enabled by default). Control behavior
with:

- `odi update` — explicit check and update
- `--no-update` flag — skip auto-update for this run
- `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1` — disable auto-update globally

When running from a non-frozen source install, auto-update is suppressed
automatically.

## Install layout

```text
~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
  ├── versions/<version>/
  │   └── odi (and bundled files)
  └── current -> versions/<version>

~/.local/bin/
  ├── odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
  ├── odipm
  ├── odi-cli
  └── agentic-odi

~/.config/agentic-odi/  # state/preferences
```

Environment variables: `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR` (override install root),
`XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_BIN_HOME`. The default backend is `local`
(`--backend local`); no MCP server is required.

## Unsigned binaries

macOS may quarantine downloaded binaries:
`xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/odi` (if needed). Windows SmartScreen
may show a warning for unsigned binaries; choose "More info → Run anyway" if you
trust the release.

## Release automation

Releases are cut and published by CI with no approval step:

1. Conventional commits land on `main`; `release-please` opens or updates the
   release PR.
2. The `release-please` workflow arms auto-merge on that PR. `main` requires the
   `CI green` check (ruleset `main-requires-ci-green`), so the PR merges itself
   as soon as CI passes — nobody clicks merge.
3. The merge cuts tag `vX.Y.Z` and the GitHub Release; the tag starts the
   `release` and `Tauri Release` workflows, which attach the CLI archives,
   `checksums.txt`, the install scripts, and the desktop bundles to it.
   The `release-instructions` job then appends an end-user "## 📦 Download &
   Run" section to the release page, listing the per-platform archives,
   `checksums.txt`, and the install scripts, plus one-line install and
   quick-run commands (idempotent on re-runs).
4. `e2e-install` runs after `release` succeeds and installs the published binary
   on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

**One-time setup (GitHub App).** GitHub holds workflow runs that start from
`GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored pushes ("This workflow requires approval from a
maintainer") and ignores the tag such a push creates, which is why releases used
to need a maintainer. A release-only GitHub App avoids both:

1. Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App, with
   permissions: Contents `Read and write`, Issues `Read and write`, Pull
   requests `Read and write` (no webhook).
2. Install the App on this repository.
3. Add repository secrets `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID` (the App's client ID)
   and `RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (a generated private key).

Until those secrets exist, the `release-please` workflow logs a warning and falls
back to `GITHUB_TOKEN`: releases still happen, but the release PR needs a
maintainer approval and merge, and the tag will not start the asset builds. After
adding the secrets, re-run the workflow (`gh workflow run release-please.yml`) or
push to `main` so the open release PR is re-driven by the App.

To check the installer without cutting a release, run
`bash scripts/tests/install_e2e.sh` — it serves a simulated release over HTTP and
exercises `scripts/install.sh` end to end (CI runs it too).

# Running The Living Studio

**The Living Studio** is the conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation:
an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact
Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous agent
connected to the MCP server.

The Studio runs three ways locally, plus a hosted deployment. All of them serve
the same SPA, which talks only to the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the
SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM directly.

## Architecture

```text
┌────────────────────────────┐  /api (JSON)  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
│  Living Studio SPA         │ ────────────▶ │  apps/studio-api (sidecar)    │
│  React + TS + Vite         │  /api/chat    │  FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100    │
│  (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │  - config / health / canvas   │
└────────────────────────────┘  SSE stream   │  - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │
                                             │  - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop)  │
                                             └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                                                             │ MCP (HTTP)
                                                             ▼
                                             ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                                             │  apps/mcp-server :8000/mcp    │
                                             └───────────────────────────────┘
                                                             ▲
                                                             │ OpenAI-compatible
                                             ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
                                             │  Your local LLM backend       │
                                             └───────────────────────────────┘
```

## Interface

The Studio opens as a conversation, not a dashboard.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| **First-run tour** | A four-step, skippable welcome on the very first visit: what the studio is, which of four starting points you want, the live state of your sidecar/MCP/model (with inline repair when the model is down), and the first move. Finishing opens the chosen surface; **Name the job** hands off to the context conversation. Replay it from **Settings → Replay the welcome tour**. |
| **First run** | A short conversation in the chat, not a form: what you are building, who feels the problem, the job they are trying to get done, then where it hurts. One question at a time, with a reflection before the next ask, quick replies, and **Explore on my own** always visible. Skipping is allowed; answers and progress are kept as a draft. Re-open it any time with `/start`, the sidebar's **Your context**, or Settings. |
| **Hero** | One rotating headline above the composer: a greeting (time of day, plus your name if you set one in Settings), the product/job you set up, what is already on the canvas, or what the studio can do. It cycles every few seconds and stays still under `prefers-reduced-motion`. |
| **Suggestion pills** | Below the headline. Some open a surface (landscape, simulate, capture), others start a conversation. They change as the canvas fills up. |
| **Composer** | Docked at the bottom of the transcript. `Enter` sends, `Shift`+`Enter` adds a line, `Cmd/Ctrl`+`K` focuses it, and `/` opens the command palette. The send button becomes a stop button while a reply streams. |
| **Drawer** (left) | The wordmark is a home button. Below it: new conversation, your context, the five workspace surfaces with counts, live model/MCP status, and Settings. Collapses to an icon rail with `Cmd/Ctrl`+`B`; becomes an overlay sheet on narrow screens. |
| **Workspace surfaces** | The classic UI — opportunity landscape, job map, impact simulation, evidence, direct capture, settings — takes the whole stage while open. **Back to conversation** or `Esc` returns; the chat is never squeezed into a side column. |

Replies render Markdown (headings, lists, emphasis, inline and fenced code).
Tool calls appear inline as small trace chips while the agent works.

### Slash commands

Type `/` to open the palette. `Up`/`Down` move, `Enter` or `Tab` runs the
selected command, `Esc` closes it. Commands are handled in the SPA and never call
the model, so they work when it is offline.

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `/help` | Every command, as a notice in the transcript |
| `/start` | Resume the context conversation |

=== tauri-release.yml ===
name: Tauri Release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Existing release tag to attach desktop bundles to (e.g. v0.3.0)"
        required: true
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: tauri-release-${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  preflight:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - name: Require updater signing key
        env:
          SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "$SIGNING_KEY" ]; then
            echo "::error::TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY is required to publish a signed release; without it the updater artifacts would be broken."
            exit 1
          fi

  build:
    needs: [preflight]
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - platform: ubuntu-22.04
            args: ""
          - platform: macos-latest
            args: "--target aarch64-apple-darwin"
          - platform: macos-latest
            args: "--target x86_64-apple-darwin"
          - platform: windows-latest
            args: ""
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.platform }}
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        if: matrix.platform == 'ubuntu-22.04'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ startsWith(matrix.platform, 'macos') && 'aarch64-apple-darwin,x86_64-apple-darwin' || '' }}

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - name: Install frontend dependencies
        run: npm ci
        working-directory: apps/studio

      - name: Import Windows signing certificate
        if: matrix.platform == 'windows-latest'
        shell: pwsh
        env:
          WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE }}
          WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if ([string]::IsNullOrEmpty($env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE)) {
            Write-Output "No WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE secret — building unsigned Windows installer."
            exit 0
          }
          $bytes = [Convert]::FromBase64String($env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE)
          $path = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP "cert.pfx"
          [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes($path, $bytes)
          $secure = ConvertTo-SecureString -String $env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD -AsPlainText -Force
          $cert = Import-PfxCertificate -FilePath $path -CertStoreLocation Cert:\CurrentUser\My -Password $secure
          $config = '{"bundle":{"windows":{"certificateThumbprint":"' + $cert.Thumbprint + '"}}}'
          "TAURI_CONFIG=$config" | Out-File -FilePath $env:GITHUB_ENV -Append -Encoding utf8
          Write-Output "Imported Windows certificate $($cert.Thumbprint)"

      # The release already exists (release-please cuts it for the tag), so this
      # attaches the desktop bundles to it and publishes it — no draft is left
      # behind for a maintainer to publish by hand.
      - name: Build and attach release
        uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@v1
        env:

          APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY: ${{ secrets.APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
        with:
          projectPath: apps/studio
          tagName: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseName: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseDraft: false
          prerelease: false
          args: ${{ matrix.args }}

"""FastAPI app for the Living Studio sidecar."""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
from pathlib import Path

from agentic_odi_core import ODIService
from agentic_odi_core.repository import Repository
from agentic_odi_core.sqlite_repository import SQLiteRepository
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.responses import FileResponse, JSONResponse
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles

from agentic_odi_studio_api.studio.connectors import ConnectorService
from agentic_odi_studio_api.studio.router import router as studio_router

CORS_ORIGINS = [
    "tauri://localhost",
    "http://tauri.localhost",
    "http://localhost:5173",
    "http://127.0.0.1:5173",
    "http://localhost:8100",
    "http://127.0.0.1:8100",
]

DEFAULT_BACKEND = "local"


def default_spa_dist() -> Path:
    """Resolve the built SPA, preferring an explicit override."""
    configured = os.environ.get("AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DIST")
    if configured:
        return Path(configured)
    return Path(__file__).resolve().parents[4] / "apps" / "studio" / "dist"


SPA_DIST = default_spa_dist()


def create_app(
    repo: Repository | None = None,
    backend: str | None = None,
    connectors: ConnectorService | None = None,
) -> FastAPI:
    if repo is None:
        repo = SQLiteRepository()
    service = ODIService(repo)
    app = FastAPI(title="Agentic ODI Studio API")
    app.state.service = service
    app.state.backend = backend or os.environ.get("AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND") or DEFAULT_BACKEND
    app.state.connectors = connectors or ConnectorService()

    app.add_middleware(
        CORSMiddleware,
        allow_origins=CORS_ORIGINS,
        allow_credentials=False,
        allow_methods=["*"],
        allow_headers=["*"],
    )

    @app.get("/health")
    def health() -> dict:
        return {"status": "ok"}

    @app.get("/capabilities")
    def capabilities() -> dict:
        return {"capabilities": app.state.backend}

    app.include_router(studio_router)

    if SPA_DIST.is_dir() and not os.getenv("AGENTIC_ODI_DISABLE_SPA"):
        assets_dir = SPA_DIST / "assets"
        if assets_dir.is_dir():
            app.mount("/assets", StaticFiles(directory=assets_dir), name="assets")

        @app.get("/{full_path:path}", response_model=None)
        def spa_fallback(full_path: str) -> FileResponse | JSONResponse:
            candidate = (SPA_DIST / full_path).resolve()
            if full_path and candidate.is_file() and candidate.is_relative_to(SPA_DIST.resolve()):
                return FileResponse(candidate)
            index = SPA_DIST / "index.html"
            if index.is_file():
                return FileResponse(index)
            return JSONResponse({"detail": "Not Found"}, status_code=404)

    return app

publishes ``website/`` is a workflow that uploads the built site and deploys the
artifact. When that workflow was removed, every check kept passing while
https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/ returned 404. These assertions keep

"""

from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
WORKFLOW = ROOT / ".github" / "workflows" / "pages.yml"

        "so without it https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/ 404s"
    )
    return WORKFLOW.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

    text = _workflow()

    assert "branches: [main]" in text

def test_grants_pages_and_oidc_permissions() -> None:
    text = _workflow()
    assert "pages: write" in text
    assert "id-token: write" in text


def test_uploads_and_deploys_the_built_site() -> None:
    text = _workflow()

    assert "website/ _site/" in text
